stem.text: The leopard, Panthera pardus, is a large mammal found in a number of countries in Africa and Asia.
Most leopards have yellow-brown fur with black spots, but 11% of leopards have black fur.
Figure 4.1 shows the two types of leopard.

stem.caption: Figure 4.1
stem.alt: Leopards with spotted yellow-brown fur and black fur.

stem.text: In the gene that controls fur colour in leopards, the allele that results in black fur is recessive.
Assuming the Hardy-Weinberg principle applies to leopard populations, calculate the percentage of leopards that are heterozygous for the gene that controls fur colour.

stem.caption: Hardy–Weinberg equations
stem.alt: Hardy–Weinberg equations and definitions of allele and genotype frequencies.

source.note: No printed figure number; caption is descriptive metadata.

stem.text: Show your working and give your answer to the nearest whole number.

explanation.text: The recessive phenotype frequency is q², not q. From q² = 0.11, find q, then p = 1 − q, and finally the heterozygote frequency 2pq.

reasoningChain: Take the square root of 0.11 and calculate p.
Calculate 2pq × 100 and round only the final percentage.

inferredMistakes.text: Using 11% as q rather than q² before calculating 2pq.

stem.text: Fur colour in leopards shows discontinuous variation. The mass of leopards shows continuous variation.
Compare the genetic basis of discontinuous variation and continuous variation.

points.text: (only) continuous, is polygenetic / involves more than two genes / involves many genes ;
in continuous different alleles have a small(er) effect (on the trait) ;
(only) continuous has, genes / alleles, showing an additive effect ;

explanation.text: Continuous variation commonly involves many genes with small additive effects. Discontinuous categories may depend on a single gene or a small number of genes with larger distinguishable effects.

reasoningChain: Compare the number and relative effects of genes.
Relate those effects to intermediate values or separate categories.

stem.text: Scientists think that the leopard populations in Asia were established by the migration of leopards from Africa approximately 500 000 years ago.
African and Asian leopards are considered to be the same species, but there are many genetic differences between them.
Suggest why there are many genetic differences between African leopards and Asian leopards.

points.text: founder effect / genetic drift ; A description
no gene flow / no interbreeding / reproductive isolation (between populations) ;

explanation.text: An isolated migrant group may begin with a non-representative allele sample. Subsequent mutation, drift and different selection pressures can increase genetic differences without necessarily completing speciation.

reasoningChain: Identify the founder effect and reduced gene flow.
Add independent causes of later divergence.
